name: System Design 101
author: Recurse
subject: cs
description: The building blocks of scalable systems: requests, latency, load balancers, caches, CDNs, replicas, queues, availability.

lesson.intro: System design is deciding how the pieces of a service fit together so it stays fast and available as it grows. This pack covers the building blocks: clients and servers, latency, load balancers, caches, CDNs, databases, queues and redundancy.
objectives: Trace a web request and explain why servers should be stateless
Use latency numbers and rough math to judge whether a design is fast enough
Explain scaling up and out, load balancing, caches and CDNs, and when each helps
Describe replication, sharding, queues and redundancy, with their trade-offs

sections.title: Clients, servers and the life of a request
sections.key: A client sends a request, and a server does the work and sends a response; keep app servers stateless so any copy can handle any request.
sections.body:
Type a web address and press Enter. In a few hundred milliseconds your browser finds a server, asks it for a page and draws the answer. Every system design is a bigger version of that **client-server** exchange:

[[visual]]

Clients never touch the database directly: the server is the gatekeeper that enforces rules, checks permissions and keeps data consistent. Most systems split the server side into **tiers**: an application tier that handles requests and a data tier (databases, caches, file storage) that remembers things, so each can grow on its own.

HTTP is **stateless**: each request stands alone, which is why every request carries a cookie or token saying who is calling. Keeping no per-user state in app server memory is the most useful habit in system design: it lets you run many identical copies.

[[code]]

messages.label: query
messages.detail: or a cache, or another service

sections.code:
$ curl -i https://example.com/api/users/42 \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi..."
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: max-age=60

{"id": 42, "name": "Ana", "plan": "pro"}
sections.pitfall: Letting clients talk to the database directly. Anyone can modify a client, so every rule about who may read or change what, and what counts as valid data, must be enforced on the server.

activity.title: Be the client
activity.prompt: List the tasks, create one, fetch it, update it and delete it, reading the status code each time. Notice that every request carries everything the server needs to handle it: the server remembers the data, not the conversation.

check.question: The signup form already checks that an email address is valid. Why must the server check it again?
choices: Servers are faster at checking than browsers
Browsers cannot run validation code
Clients can be modified or bypassed, so only checks on the server can be trusted
HTTP requires every field to be validated twice
check.explanation: Anyone can skip the form and send a request directly with any data they like. Client-side checks are for a friendly experience; server-side checks are for correctness and security.

sections.title: Latency numbers and back-of-the-envelope estimates
sections.key: Rough latencies and rounded arithmetic tell you whether a design is fast enough: a round trip costs about 0.5 ms inside a data center but about 150 ms across continents.
sections.body:
Is a page that makes 20 database queries fast? Twenty round trips inside one data center cost about 10 ms; twenty to another continent cost about 3 seconds. The **ratios** are what matter:

[[visual]]

- **Avoid round trips**: batch small requests, and run independent calls in parallel.
- **Keep hot data in memory**: a RAM cache answers in microseconds, a database in milliseconds.
- **Put data near users**: light in fiber covers about 200 km per millisecond.

Rough arithmetic also gives **back-of-the-envelope estimates**. Round hard: a day has 86,400 seconds, so call it 10^5.

[[visual 2]]

Estimates make requirements concrete. **Functional** requirements say what the system does; **non-functional** ones say how well, and they drive most design decisions:

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Rough latencies

items.label: Round trip in one data center

visual.caption: RAM is about 100 times slower than L1, an SSD about 1,000 times slower than RAM, and a cross-continent trip about 1,000 times slower again.

steps.label: 20 million requests a day
steps.note: peaks are often 2 to 10 times the average

steps.label: 1 million uploads a day at 2 MB each
steps.note: about 730 TB a year, before replication

items.title: Functional
points: Users see a feed of friends' posts

items.title: Non-functional
points: Up 99.9% of the time; no data ever lost

sections.pitfall: Making calls one after another that could run in parallel. Five independent 100 ms calls take 500 ms in sequence but about 100 ms together. When a page is slow, look for sequential round trips first.

check.question: Why does a request from Europe to a server in California take at least tens of milliseconds, however fast the server is?
choices: Undersea cables are limited to dial-up speeds
DNS lookups always take 100 ms
Servers in California run on slower hardware
Light in fiber covers only about 200 km per millisecond, and the path is thousands of kilometers each way
check.explanation: About 9,000 km each way at roughly 200 km per millisecond is around 45 ms one way and 90 ms for the round trip, before any routing or processing. No server upgrade can beat physics; moving data closer (a CDN or a nearby region) can.

sections.title: Scaling up, scaling out, and load balancing
sections.key: Scale up first because it needs no code changes; scale out behind a load balancer for capacity and redundancy, once the servers are stateless.
sections.body:
Your app launches, traffic doubles weekly, and the single server sits at 90 percent CPU. Two options:

[[visual]]

Scaling out needs **stateless** servers: sessions, uploads and caches move to shared stores, or a user who logged in on server 1 is a stranger to server 2. A **load balancer** then spreads requests across the copies:

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

It also runs **health checks**, probing each server every few seconds and dropping failing ones. **Layer 4** balancers route by IP and port and are very fast; **layer 7** balancers understand HTTP, so they route by path, terminate TLS and retry. Run the balancer redundantly too.

items.title: Scale up
points: No code or architecture changes: often the right first move
Has a ceiling, and prices climb steeply near the top

items.title: Scale out
points: Needs a load balancer and stateless servers

visual.title: Balancing strategies
rows: pick the server with the fewest requests in flight
some requests are far slower than others
by client IP or user ID: the same client hits the same server
servers keep local caches; load is less even

sections.pitfall: Scaling out stateful servers. If sessions, uploaded files or in-process caches live on one machine, adding machines breaks users at random. Move state to shared stores first, then add servers.

check.question: Which is an advantage of scaling up over scaling out?
choices: It has no upper limit
It removes the single point of failure
It needs no code or architecture changes
It makes the servers stateless
check.explanation: A bigger machine runs the same code unchanged, which is why teams often scale up first. It does have a ceiling, and one machine is still one point of failure; those are the reasons to scale out later.

sections.title: Caching layers
sections.key: A cache keeps copies of expensive results in fast storage; in cache-aside the app checks the cache, loads from the database on a miss, and invalidates on every write.
sections.body:
A news home page is requested 10,000 times a minute and changes a few times an hour. A **cache** keeps a copy of expensive results in fast storage, and caches sit at every layer:

[[visual]]

In application code the usual pattern is **cache-aside**:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

The **hit rate** decides how much it helps: with 1 ms hits and 20 ms misses, 90 percent hits average 0.9 × 1 + 0.1 × 20 = 2.9 ms. A full cache **evicts** entries, usually the **least recently used (LRU)**. The hard part is freshness:

[[visual 3]]

Skip caching data that must be exactly current (a balance before a payment) or is read only once.

layers.label: Browser cache
layers.detail: keeps files per HTTP headers such as `Cache-Control: max-age=3600`

layers.label: CDN
layers.detail: edge servers near users keep static files and shareable pages

layers.label: Application cache
layers.detail: Redis or Memcached, shared by all app servers: query results, fragments, sessions

layers.label: Database cache
layers.detail: the database keeps hot pages in memory

visual.arrowLabel: A request goes only as deep as its first hit

steps.label: Read the key from the cache
Is it there?
steps.no: Miss: load it from the database

steps.label: Store it in the cache with a **TTL** (time to live)
Return it; the next read is a hit

rows: bounds staleness, but users may see old data until it expires
delete the key when data changes so the next read reloads it: the usual default
when a hot key expires, thousands miss at once; let one request rebuild while others wait or get the old copy, and add jitter to TTLs

sections.code:
def get_product(pid):
    key = f"product:{pid}"
    cached = cache.get(key)    # ~1 ms
    if cached is not None:
        return json.loads(cached)   # hit
    product = db.query_one(
        "SELECT * FROM products"
        " WHERE id = %s", (pid,))
    cache.set(key, json.dumps(product),
              ex=300)          # 5 minutes
    return product

def update_price(pid, price):
    db.execute(
        "UPDATE products SET price = %s"
        " WHERE id = %s", (price, pid))
    # invalidate on write
    cache.delete(f"product:{pid}")
sections.deeper: Cache-aside leaves the application in charge: it reads the cache, falls back to the database and fills the cache itself, so the cache only ever holds data someone asked for. In **read-through** caching the cache library loads from the database on a miss by itself, and in **write-through** every write goes to the cache and the database together. With 99 percent hits in the example above, the average drops to about 1.2 ms.
sections.pitfall: Updating the database and forgetting the cache. Users then see stale data until the TTL runs out. Every write path for cached data must invalidate or update its key.

check.question: In the cache-aside pattern, what happens on a cache miss?
choices: The request fails with an error
The cache fetches the data from the database by itself
The app returns empty data until the cache warms up
The app loads the data from the database, stores it in the cache and returns it
check.explanation: In cache-aside the application owns the logic: read the cache, fall back to the database, then populate the cache for next time. A cache that loads from the database on its own is a different pattern, read-through.

sections.title: CDNs: content at the edge
sections.key: A CDN serves content from edge servers near users: the first request in a region fetches the file from the origin, and later requests there are local hits.
sections.body:
A video site hosted in Virginia serves a viewer in Sydney: every image, script and video chunk crosses the Pacific at about 200 ms a round trip. A **content delivery network (CDN)** keeps copies on **edge servers** in hundreds of cities. Your static domain points at the CDN, and DNS or anycast routes each user to a nearby edge:

[[visual]]

- **Lower latency**: content travels a short distance.
- **Less load on the origin**: popular files are absorbed at the edge.
- **Resilience**: CDNs soak up spikes and many denial-of-service attacks.

CDNs suit **static assets** (images, CSS, JavaScript, fonts, video segments) and pages that are the same for everyone. Personalized responses usually still go to the origin. Headers control caching, and versioned file names handle new releases (**cache busting**):

[[visual 2]]

items.title: Hashed asset
points: A content change makes a new name, so a new URL no cache has seen

items.title: The HTML that links to it
points: So it always points at the current asset names

visual.caption: CDNs also offer explicit purges, but versioned names are faster and more reliable.

sections.pitfall: Caching files under a fixed name with a long max-age. After you deploy a fix, browsers and edges keep serving the old file until it expires. Use content-hashed names for long-lived assets.

check.question: A viewer in Sydney requests an image the Sydney edge server has never served. What happens?
choices: The request fails until the CDN is reconfigured
The edge fetches it from the origin, caches it and serves it; later Sydney requests are hits
The viewer is permanently redirected to the origin for that image
Every edge server in the world downloads the image first
check.explanation: CDN edges fill lazily: the first request in a region pays the trip to the origin, and later requests there are served locally until the cached copy expires.

sections.title: Databases and replication
sections.key: Replicas spread reads and stand by for failover but lag behind the primary; shard data by a well-spread key only when one primary cannot cope.
sections.body:
Accounts, orders and messages must not be lost, and the database is the hardest part to scale because it is full of state.

[[visual]]

The first scaling tool is **replication**. In a **primary-replica** setup all writes go to the primary, which streams changes to replicas. Reads spread across replicas, and if the primary dies a replica is **promoted**:

[[visual 2]]

Replication is usually **asynchronous**: the primary confirms a write before replicas have it. That keeps writes fast, with costs:

[[visual 3]]

During a network **partition**, the **CAP theorem** forces a choice: **consistency** (refuse requests that could conflict) or **availability** (answer and reconcile later). Banks choose consistency; carts and feeds often choose availability with **eventual consistency**.

items.title: Relational (SQL)
points: Tables with a fixed schema, joins, flexible queries
**ACID transactions**: a transfer debits and credits completely or not at all

items.title: NoSQL
points: Trade some features for scale or flexibility
Huge volumes of lookups by key, loose records, heavy writes

rows: a replica read misses a write you just made
read a user's own recent writes from the primary
the primary crashes before shipping confirmed writes; a promoted replica never had them
**synchronous** replication, at the cost of slower writes
Too many writes for one primary
the primary or its disk cannot keep up
**shard**: split data by a **shard key** such as a hash of user_id; a bad key makes a hot shard, and cross-shard queries get hard

sections.pitfall: Reading from a replica right after a write. Even a second of lag makes a user's own change seem to vanish. Send a user's reads to the primary for a short while after they write.

check.question: What is the main benefit of adding read replicas?
choices: Spreading read traffic across machines, with a standby that can take over if the primary fails
Faster writes, because each replica accepts some of the writes
No more need for backups
A guarantee that every read sees the latest write
check.explanation: Replicas multiply read capacity and provide failover. All writes still go through the primary, replicas can lag behind it, and they faithfully copy mistakes too, so backups are still needed.

sections.title: Queues and asynchronous work
sections.key: A queue lets a request hand slow work to background workers, keeping responses fast and absorbing spikes; at-least-once delivery means every consumer must be idempotent.
sections.body:
A user uploads a video, and transcoding takes four minutes. You cannot hold the request open that long, so the handler saves the file, puts a message on a **queue** and answers at once. **Workers** take messages off and do the work at their own pace:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Most queues deliver **at least once**: a message comes back if the worker does not **acknowledge** it, say after a crash halfway through. So consumers must be **idempotent**: handling a message twice has the same effect as once (record charged order IDs and skip repeats; prefer upserts).

Messages that keep failing go to a **dead-letter queue** for a person to inspect.

[[code]]

In **publish/subscribe**, one event ("order placed") reaches several independent subscribers: billing, email, analytics. Queues make a system **eventually consistent**, so show users progress.

messages.label: ack
messages.detail: only now is the message removed

visual.title: What a queue buys
rows: the request does the quick part; emails, image work, reports and webhooks run in the background
10,000 jobs wait in line instead of overwhelming anything; add workers when the backlog grows
if a worker or downstream service is down, the message waits and is retried
producers and consumers deploy and scale separately, even in different languages
visual.caption: Common queues: RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS, Kafka, Redis-based queues.

sections.pitfall: Assuming each message is processed exactly once. With at-least-once delivery, a crash between doing the work and acknowledging the message means the work runs again. Make every consumer idempotent.

check.question: Why does at-least-once delivery require idempotent consumers?
choices: Because queues reorder messages at random
Because idempotent code runs faster
Because the queue deletes each message before it is processed
Because a message can arrive more than once, for example after a worker crashes before acknowledging it
check.explanation: The queue cannot tell whether a worker that died finished the job, so it delivers the message again. If processing twice charged a customer twice, the duplicate would be a real bug; idempotency makes the repeat harmless.

sections.title: Availability: designing for failure
sections.key: Availability comes from surviving failures: remove single points of failure with redundancy, since required parts in series multiply availability and parallel copies multiply failure odds.
sections.body:
At scale something is always broken: a dead disk, a rebooting server, a bad deploy, a data center without power. **Availability** is the fraction of time the system works, quoted in **nines**:

[[visual]]

The core technique is **redundancy**: remove every **single point of failure** (SPOF), any component whose failure takes everything down. Run two or more of everything that matters (app servers, a database replica for **failover**, paired load balancers), spread across separate **availability zones**. The arithmetic shows why:

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.caption: Each extra nine is ten times harder to reach.

steps.label: **Series**: a request needs all of them, so multiply availabilities
steps.note: every extra required dependency lowers it

steps.label: **Parallel**: any one copy is enough, so multiply the failure chances
steps.note: real failures correlate, so put copies in separate zones

visual.title: Habits of reliable systems
rows: a dead component is noticed in seconds, not when users complain
a slow dependency does not tie up every thread, and retries do not become a flood
return **429 Too Many Requests** past a quota; a **token bucket** allows bursts up to its size, then refills at a steady rate
if recommendations are down, show the page without them
replication faithfully copies a mistaken `DELETE` too

sections.pitfall: Retrying instantly and forever. When a dependency struggles, thousands of clients retrying at once keep it down. Use timeouts, a few retries with exponential backoff and jitter, then give up gracefully.

check.question: The app tier and the database are each 99.9% available, and every request needs both. You add a cache (99.9% available) that every request must also pass through. What happens to overall availability?
choices: It rises, because caches make requests faster
It falls to about 99.7%, because one more required component multiplies in
It stays the same, because all three are 99.9%
It rises to 99.99%, because there are more components
check.explanation: Required components in series multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 is about 0.997. A cache helps speed and database load, but only if a cache outage degrades gracefully to the database instead of failing the request.

keyTerms.definition: A server that keeps no per-user state in its own memory between requests, so any copy can handle any request.
How long one operation or request takes, from start to finish.
Scaling up: moving to a bigger machine. Simple, but capped and still a single point of failure.
Scaling out: adding more machines running the same code behind a load balancer.
A component that spreads incoming requests across healthy servers using round robin, least connections or hashing.
Read the cache; on a miss, load from the database, store the result with a TTL and return it. Invalidate the key on writes.
A content delivery network: edge servers worldwide that cache content close to users.
The delay before a write on the primary appears on a replica, which can make recent writes seem missing.
Splitting data across several databases by a shard key, such as a hash of the user ID.
A buffer between producers and consumers that lets slow work run in the background and absorbs spikes.
Safe to repeat: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Required for consumers with at-least-once delivery.
A component whose failure takes the whole system down. Removed with redundancy and failover.

summary: Clients send requests and servers respond; keep servers stateless so any copy can serve any request.
Know rough latencies (RAM 100 ns, SSD 100 µs, data center round trip 0.5 ms, cross-continent 150 ms) and avoid sequential round trips.
Scale up first, then scale out behind a load balancer with health checks.
Cache at every layer and invalidate on write; CDNs serve static files from the edge with hashed names.
Replicas spread reads and allow failover but lag; shard only when one primary cannot cope.
Queues absorb spikes for idempotent workers; redundancy, timeouts and rate limits keep a system up.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how a photo-sharing app could grow from 100 users on one server to 10 million users, naming each piece you would add (load balancer, cache, CDN, database replicas, queue) and the problem each one solves.

questions.question: A service receives 50 million requests per day, spread evenly. Using 1 day = 100,000 seconds, about how many requests per second is that?
questions.explanation: 50,000,000 / 100,000 = 500 requests per second. The exact figure with 86,400 seconds is about 579, but the rounded 10^5 is close enough for design decisions. Peaks will be higher than this average.

questions.question: Which of these is a non-functional requirement?
choices: Users can upload a profile photo
Users can follow other users
95% of feed loads finish in under 200 ms
Admins can delete any post
questions.explanation: A latency target describes how well the system performs, which makes it non-functional. The others describe features the system offers, which are functional requirements.

questions.question: Users upload 2 million photos a day, averaging 500 KB each. Roughly how much new storage is needed per day?
choices: About 1 TB
About 1 GB
About 100 GB
About 10 TB
questions.explanation: 2 x 10^6 photos x 500 x 10^3 bytes = 10^12 bytes, which is 1 TB per day, or about 365 TB a year before replication. Getting 1 GB means dropping a factor of 1,000 somewhere in the units.

questions.question: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling: give one advantage and one limitation of each.
questions.answer: Vertical scaling (a bigger machine) needs no code changes, but it hits a hardware ceiling and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (more machines) has no hard ceiling and survives losing a machine, but servers must be stateless and you need a load balancer.
questions.explanation: Teams often scale up first because it is simple, and scale out once they need more capacity or redundancy than one machine can give.

questions.question: After a second app server was added behind the load balancer, users get logged out at random. What is wrong?
questions.code:
# load balancer: round robin
upstream app {
    server 10.0.0.11:8080;   # app-1
    server 10.0.0.12:8080;   # app-2
}

# app server
sessions = {}                      # in-process memory
on login:   sessions[token] = user
on request: user = sessions.get(token)   # null -> redirect to login
choices: Round robin is faulty; switching to random selection fixes it
Sessions live in each server's memory, so the other one has no session
The two app servers must listen on different port numbers
The load balancer should cache the login page separately for each user
questions.explanation: A user who logged in on app-1 has no session on app-2, and round robin alternates between them. Make the servers stateless by moving sessions to a shared store such as Redis or into signed tokens. Random selection would fail the same way.

questions.question: Some requests to a service take 20 ms and others take 30 seconds. Which load balancing algorithm spreads the work most evenly?
choices: Round robin
Random selection
Hashing on the client IP
Least connections
questions.explanation: Least connections sends each new request to the server with the fewest requests in flight, so a server stuck on slow requests gets fewer new ones. Round robin hands out equal counts, which can pile slow requests onto one server.

questions.question: Complete the cache-aside read so the next request for this user is a cache hit.
choices: db.update("users", id, user)
cache.delete("user:" + id)
cache.set("user:" + id, user, 300)
user = cache.get("user:" + id)
questions.explanation: After a miss, cache-aside stores the value it just loaded, here with a 300-second TTL, so later reads skip the database. Deleting the key is what you do after a write, not after a read.

questions.question: A user renames their profile but keeps seeing the old name for up to 10 minutes. Profiles are cached with a 10-minute TTL. What is the most direct fix?
choices: Delete the profile's cache key whenever it is updated
Raise the TTL to one hour so the cache is hit more often
Add a read replica for the profiles table to share load
Switch the cache's eviction policy from FIFO to LRU
questions.explanation: Invalidating the key on write means the next read misses and loads the new name. A longer TTL makes staleness worse, and eviction policy only matters when the cache is full.

questions.question: The cached home page expires every 5 minutes, and each time thousands of requests miss at once and overload the database. Which fix targets this problem?
choices: Lower the TTL to 10 seconds so the page stays fresher
Stop caching the home page and always query the database
Add more app servers to absorb the extra requests
Let one request rebuild it while others wait or use the old copy
questions.explanation: This is a cache stampede. Making only one request recompute the value keeps the database load to a single query. A shorter TTL causes stampedes more often, and more app servers send even more simultaneous queries.

questions.question: A user posts a comment and refreshes; the comment is missing, then appears a second later. Reads are served by replicas. What is happening?
choices: The first write failed and the app retried it a second later
Replication lag: the replica had not received the write yet
The cache evicted the comment and had to reload it
The shard key is unbalanced, so one shard answered slowly
questions.explanation: With asynchronous replication, the primary has the write but the replica serving the read is slightly behind. Reading a user's own recent writes from the primary avoids this.

questions.question: You are sharding a users table across 8 database servers. Which shard key spreads data and traffic most evenly?
choices: Country
Signup date, one date range per shard
A hash of user_id
Account type (free or paid)
questions.explanation: Hashing a high-cardinality key like user_id scatters users evenly. Country puts big countries on one hot shard, date ranges send every new signup to the newest shard, and account type has only two values for 8 shards.

questions.question: During a network partition, a bank's replicated ledger rejects writes on the side that cannot reach a majority, rather than risk conflicting balances. Which CAP trade-off is this?
choices: Consistency over availability
Availability over consistency
Partition tolerance over consistency
Eventual consistency
questions.explanation: Refusing requests to avoid conflicting data keeps the system consistent at the cost of availability. An available design would accept writes on both sides and reconcile later, which is eventual consistency.

questions.question: Which workload most clearly calls for a relational database with ACID transactions?
choices: Caching rendered web pages for a few minutes at a time
Storing a stream of click events for later analysis
Looking up short-lived session data by its session ID
A money transfer where both account updates succeed or neither does
questions.explanation: A transfer must debit one account and credit the other atomically, which is exactly what ACID transactions guarantee. Caches, event streams and session lookups fit key-value or append-only stores well.

questions.question: Sending the welcome email during sign-up sometimes takes 5 seconds, which makes sign-up slow. What is the standard fix?
choices: Move the email code to a bigger, faster dedicated server of its own
Put an email job on a queue and let a background worker send it
Cache the welcome email so it is generated only once
Skip sending the email whenever the server is under load
questions.explanation: The request only needs to enqueue the job, which takes milliseconds; a worker sends the email afterward and can retry if the provider is down. A bigger server does not make the email provider respond faster.

questions.question: Occasionally a customer is charged twice for one order. What is wrong with this worker?
questions.code:
# worker; the queue guarantees at-least-once delivery
loop:
    msg = queue.receive()
    payments.charge(msg.order_id, msg.amount)
    queue.ack(msg)
choices: The queue is too slow, so duplicate messages pile up in it
Calling ack before charging would fix it with no downside
Redelivery after a crash before ack; skip orders already charged
The worker must sleep between messages to avoid reading one twice
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery means a message can arrive twice, so the worker must skip orders it already charged. Acking first just swaps the bug: a crash after the ack would lose the payment entirely.

questions.question: Which HTTP status code should an API return when a client has exceeded its rate limit?
questions.explanation: 429 Too Many Requests tells the client to slow down, ideally with a Retry-After header saying when to try again. 503 means the server itself is unavailable, which is a different message.

questions.question: A token bucket holds at most 10 tokens and refills 1 token per second. A client has been idle for a minute, then sends 15 requests at the same instant. How many are allowed?
questions.explanation: The bucket refilled during the idle minute but stops at its capacity of 10. The burst spends all 10 tokens, and the other 5 requests are rejected until tokens refill at 1 per second.

questions.question: What does it mean for an application server to be stateless?
choices: It keeps no per-user data in its own memory between requests, so any server can handle any request
It stores no data anywhere, not even in a database
It can only serve static files
It forgets its configuration after every restart
questions.explanation: Stateless servers keep sessions and other state in shared stores (a database, Redis, signed tokens). The data still exists, just not inside one server, which is what makes adding or replacing servers safe.

questions.question: Put the steps of loading https://example.com/profile in order.
items: Resolve example.com to an IP address with DNS
Open a TCP connection and set up TLS
Send the HTTP request with its method, path and headers
The server runs application code, which may read a cache or database
The server returns an HTTP response with a status code and body
questions.explanation: The client needs an address before it can connect, and a connection (with TLS for HTTPS) before it can send a request. Everything a system design adds, from load balancers to caches, sits inside the fourth step.

questions.question: Match each operation with its rough latency.

pairs.left: Round trip inside one data center
Round trip from California to Europe

questions.explanation: Each step down the list is roughly 100 to 1,000 times slower than the one before. Memorizing the orders of magnitude is enough to spot designs that make too many slow trips.

questions.question: A request handler calls a service in another region three times, one call after another, and each round trip takes 100 ms. At minimum, how many milliseconds do those calls add?
questions.explanation: Sequential calls add up: 3 × 100 ms = 300 ms. If the calls do not depend on each other, making them in parallel cuts that to about 100 ms.

questions.question: Your only database server is at 90% CPU. Which of these is scaling up?
choices: Adding two read replicas
Putting a load balancer in front of it
Splitting the data across four shards
Moving it to a machine with more cores and more RAM
questions.explanation: Scaling up means a bigger machine. Replicas and shards add machines, which is scaling out, and a load balancer spreads traffic across machines you already have.

questions.question: What does a load balancer's health check do?
choices: Measures the quality of the network cables
Probes each server regularly and stops sending traffic to servers that fail
Restarts servers that use too much memory
Checks that users are logged in before forwarding requests
questions.explanation: Health checks turn a crashed server from an outage for some users into a non-event: the balancer simply stops routing to it until it recovers. Restarting servers is the job of other tooling.

questions.question: Which of these are good candidates for caching? Select all that apply.
choices: A product page viewed 10,000 times a minute that changes once a day
An expensive report query whose result may be a few minutes old
A customer's account balance, read just before approving a payment
Static images and JavaScript files
A one-time login code the user just received
questions.explanation: Caching pays off for data that is read far more often than it changes and can tolerate brief staleness. A balance checked before a payment must be exact, and a one-time code is read once, so caching either one adds risk and saves nothing.

questions.question: A cache hit takes 2 ms and a miss (check the cache, then query the database) takes 50 ms. With an 80% hit rate, what is the average latency in ms?
questions.explanation: 0.8 × 2 + 0.2 × 50 = 1.6 + 10 = 11.6 ms. The misses dominate: raising the hit rate to 95% would bring the average down to about 4.4 ms.

questions.question: What is the main job of a CDN?
choices: Serving content from edge servers near users, cutting latency and load on the origin
Replicating the primary database to other regions
Balancing traffic between app servers inside one data center
Storing user sessions
questions.explanation: A CDN caches content in many locations so most requests travel a short distance and never reach your servers. Database replication and load balancing are separate tools.

questions.question: You deploy a fixed app.js, but users keep getting the old file from the CDN for hours. What is the standard long-term fix?
choices: Lower the CDN TTL for every file to 5 seconds
Ask users to clear their browser caches
Turn the CDN off during deployments
Put a content hash in asset file names, such as app.3f9a1c.js, so each version gets a new URL
questions.explanation: A new name is a new cache entry, so the fix reaches users immediately while unchanged files stay cached for a year. Tiny TTLs throw away most of the CDN's benefit, and you cannot rely on users clearing caches.

questions.question: A primary database replicates asynchronously. It acknowledges a write, then crashes before shipping it, and a replica is promoted. What happens to that write?
choices: The new primary fetches it from the crashed primary's memory
It is lost, even though the client was told it succeeded
The client's browser replays it automatically
The promotion waits until the write arrives
questions.explanation: Asynchronous replication confirms writes before any replica has them, so a crash can lose the most recent ones. Synchronous replication, or waiting for at least one replica to confirm, closes that gap at the cost of slower writes.

questions.question: What is a dead-letter queue for?
choices: Messages waiting for a worker to become free
Messages that were processed successfully
Messages that failed repeatedly, set aside for inspection instead of being retried forever
Messages that are sent to every subscriber at once
questions.explanation: A message that crashes its worker every time (a poison message) would otherwise be retried endlessly and block other work. Moving it aside keeps the queue flowing and lets a person find the bug.

questions.question: 99.9% availability allows roughly how many hours of downtime per year?
questions.explanation: A year has 8,760 hours, and 0.1% of that is 8.76 hours. Each extra nine cuts it tenfold: 99.99% allows about 53 minutes a year.

questions.question: Every request passes through four services, each 99.9% available, and fails if any one is down. Roughly what is the availability of the whole path?
choices: About 99.6%
About 96%
questions.explanation: Required components in series multiply: 0.999^4 is about 0.996, or 99.6%, which is roughly 35 hours of downtime a year. Every hard dependency you add lowers availability, which is why critical paths are kept short.

questions.question: What is a single point of failure, and how do you remove one?
questions.answer: A component whose failure takes the whole system down, such as a lone database or load balancer. You remove it with redundancy: run two or more instances, ideally in separate availability zones, with health checks and automatic failover.
questions.explanation: Redundancy only helps if failover actually works, so reliable teams test it, for example by deliberately shutting down an instance and watching traffic move.

questions.question: Why do requests to a web API carry a cookie or token on every call?
choices: Cookies make requests travel faster
TCP requires a token on every packet
Servers collect tokens only for analytics
HTTP is stateless, so each request must tell the server who is calling
questions.explanation: The server does not remember earlier requests, and with several stateless servers the next request may land somewhere else entirely. The cookie or token lets whichever server receives it identify the user.
